questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old patient with known cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis C presents with new-onset ascites. Diagnostic paracentesis is performed. Serum albumin is 3.0 g/dL, and ascitic fluid albumin is 1.8 g/dL. What is the most likely etiology of the ascites based on the Serum Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG)?
questions.solution: Explanation: The Serum Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) is a highly accurate tool for classifying the etiology of ascites. It is calculated by subtracting the ascitic fluid albumin concentration from the serum albumin concentration obtained simultaneously (SAAG = serum albumin – ascitic fluid albumin). In this patient, SAAG = 3.0 g/dL (serum) - 1.8 g/dL (ascitic fluid) = 1.2 g/dL. A SAAG value of ≥ 1.1 g/dL is highly suggestive of portal hypertension as the cause of ascites, typically due to advanced liver disease like cirrhosis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Peritoneal carcinomatosis: This would typically result in a low SAAG (<1.1 g/dL) because the ascites is caused by fluid leakage from peritoneal tumor implants, not portal hypertension. questions.solution: g>Explanation: Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt (TIPS) placement is a standard procedure for managing complications of portal hypertension in patients with decompensated cirrhosis, particularly recurrent ascites and variceal rebleeding. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Residual Volume (RV): Simple spirometry measures volumes of air that can be moved in and out of the lungs. Residual Volume (RV) is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a maximal exhalation and cannot be exhaled; therefore, it cannot be measured by spirometry.
